findings.antecedent: Contact with nature (based on biophilia hypothesis)
findings.consequent: Basic human need (universal primary need)
findings.quote: If there is an evolutionary basis for biophilia, as asserted by E.O. Wilson in the opening quote, then contact with nature is a basic human need: not a cultural amenity, not an individual preference, but a universal primary need.

findings.antecedent: Ongoing connections with the natural world
findings.consequent: Human flourishing (well-being)
findings.quote: Just as we need healthy food and regular exercise to flourish, we need ongoing connections with the natural world.

findings.antecedent: Experience of nature across evolutionary time periods
findings.consequent: Marks on human minds, behavioral patterns, and physiological functioning
findings.quote: The experience of nature across evolutionary time periods has left its mark on our minds, our behavioral patterns, and our physiological functioning.

findings.antecedent: Nature's forms, processes, and patterns
findings.consequent: Powerful human responsiveness (as a species)
findings.quote: The biophilia hypothesis and supporting research tells us that, as a species, we are still powerfully responsive to nature's forms, processes, and patterns

findings.antecedent: Knowledge of human affinity for nature (biophilia)
findings.consequent: Generation of health and wellness experiences through created environments
findings.quote: Using knowledge of our affinity for nature, adapted and refined over millions of years, we can generate experiences of health and wellness through the environments we create.

findings.antecedent: Natural landscape (ancestral life)
findings.consequent: Provision of resources necessary for human survival (water, sunlight, food, building materials, shelter, vistas, fire)
findings.quote: For the vast majority of human existence, the natural landscape provided the resources necessary for human survival, chief among them water, sunlight, animal and vegetable food, building materials, shelter, vistas, and fire.

findings.antecedent: Daily connection to nature
findings.consequent: Reinforcement of values of respect and care for the environment
findings.quote: Connection to nature on a daily basis reinforces the values of respect and care for the environment that are necessities for sustainable communities.

findings.antecedent: Spaces with dead and dying plants and trees
findings.consequent: Avoidance; signal of habitat depletion
findings.quote: However, not all nature is equally attractive or beneficial. Spaces with dead and dying plants and trees signal habitat depletion and are largely avoided.

findings.antecedent: Places with rich vegetation, flowers, large trees, water, and meandering pathways
findings.consequent: Sought out for relaxation and enjoyment
findings.quote: In contrast, places with rich vegetation, flowers, large trees, water, and meandering pathways that open suddenly to views are sought out by many as places of relaxation and enjoyment.

findings.antecedent: Nature contact (across research studies)
findings.consequent: Improved moods and reduced stress
findings.quote: Improved moods and reduced stress are the most consistent benefits of nature contact across research studies

findings.antecedent: Nature contact (visual, multi-sensory, active, passive; across settings, cultures, ages)
findings.consequent: Benefits (improved mood, reduced stress)
findings.quote: Furthermore, contact with nature can be purely visual or multi-sensory, active engagement (walking, running, gardening) or passive (viewing only). Benefits are found in multiple settings, multiple cultures, and across the age span, from early childhood to late adulthood.

findings.antecedent: Hospital patients with window views of outdoor landscapes (trees)
findings.consequent: Less narcotic and milder analgesic use, shorter hospital stays, more positive post-surgical recovery
findings.quote: Ulrich found that patients with the tree view used less narcotic and milder analgesics, indicating lower pain experience. They also stayed in the hospital for a shorter time period and had a more positive post-surgical recovery overall than did patients who had the view of the brick wall.

findings.antecedent: Exposure to nature scenes (real or simulated) after a stressor
findings.consequent: Faster and more positive recovery (physiological stress reduction, mood enhancement)
key_citations: Ulrich and colleagues, Texas A&M University
findings.quote: Subjects exposed to a stressor recover faster and more positively if they are shown nature scenes or urban scenes with nature, rather than urban scenes devoid of natural elements. Subjects viewing the completely natural scenes do the best overall, with the greatest and most rapid reduction in physiological stress and more rapid mood enhancement.

findings.antecedent: Windowless offices
findings.consequent: Increased use of nature elements (posters, photos) for decoration
findings.quote: They found that people in windowless spaces used twice as many nature elements (posters and photos especially) to decorate their office walls than those who had window views to natural areas outdoors.

findings.antecedent: Daylight environments
findings.consequent: Preference and belief in better health and psychological functioning
findings.quote: We have known for a long time that people prefer daylight environments and that they believe daylight is better for health and psychological functioning than is electric light.

findings.antecedent: Bright daylight
findings.consequent: Medicinal properties: entrains circadian rhythms, enhances mood, promotes neurological health, affects alertness
findings.quote: We know now that bright daylight has medicinal properties. It entrains circadian rhythms, enhances mood, promotes neurological health, and affects alertness.

findings.antecedent: Hospital patients in bright rooms (sunlight)
findings.consequent: More rapid recovery, reduced pain levels, fewer strong analgesics, shorter hospital stays
findings.quote: Research in hospital settings shows that patients in bright rooms recover more rapidly from illness, show reduced pain levels, take fewer strong analgesics, and stay in the hospital fewer days than patients who are in more dimly lit rooms located on the north side or in locations where nearby buildings block sun penetration

findings.antecedent: Large trees close at hand (in public housing)
findings.consequent: Attraction of people outdoors, increased neighbor interaction, stronger social bonds
findings.quote: the researchers found that housing developments with large trees attracted people to be outdoors and, once there, they talked to their neighbors and developed stronger social bonds than people in similar housing projects without green space and trees.

findings.antecedent: Children performing activities in green settings ('green time')
findings.consequent: Reduced symptoms of Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD)
findings.quote: children performing activities in green settings have shown reduced symptoms of Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder

findings.antecedent: Proximity to green spaces (household gardens, neighborhood parks, large green spaces)
findings.consequent: Better health profiles (physical, mental health, social safety)
findings.quote: the researchers have found preliminary evidence that residents who are closer to green spaces, including household gardens and neighborhood parks as well as large green spaces, have better health profiles than residents who are farther away.

findings.antecedent: Active and passive contact with gardens
findings.consequent: Psychological, emotional, and social benefits (stress recovery, escape, improved moods)
findings.quote: benefits of gardens include recovery from stress, having a place to escape to, and improved moods.

findings.antecedent: Horticulture therapy (in clinical settings and nursing homes)
findings.consequent: Improved mobility, dexterity, confidence, and social skills (in dementia and stroke patients)
findings.quote: Other studies provide evidence that dementia and stroke patients show improved mobility and dexterity, more confidence, and improved social skills as a result of gardening activities.

findings.antecedent: Gardens containing rich foliage, flowers, a water feature, congruent nature sounds (bird songs, moving water), and visible wildlife (birds)
findings.consequent: Increased calming and stress amelioration
findings.quote: According to Ulrich, gardens will be more likely to be calming and to ameliorate stress if they contain rich foliage, flowers, a water feature, congruent nature sounds (bird songs, moving water), and visible wildlife, particularly birds.

findings.antecedent: Viewing pleasant nature scenes (rural and urban)
findings.consequent: Higher self-esteem (compared to totally urban or 'unpleasant' rural scenes)
findings.quote: subjects who viewed pleasant nature scenes (both rural and urban) scored higher in measures of self-esteem than those viewing totally urban scenes or 'unpleasant' rural scenes with destroyed landscapes

findings.antecedent: Walking in an urban environment with nature
findings.consequent: Stress reduction (compared to similar walk without natural elements)
findings.quote: Similar results have been found in field studies by Hartig and colleagues (1991) who looked at the stress reducing effects of walking in an urban environment with nature as compared to a similar walk without natural elements.

findings.antecedent: Playing in natural environments (home, school, camp)
findings.consequent: Sustained benefits for social, emotional, and cognitive development in children
findings.quote: Playing in outdoor environments, whether at home, school, or camp, has sustained benefits for social, emotional, and cognitive development in children.

findings.antecedent: Nature providing platform and objects for play
findings.consequent: Encouragement of exploration, building, aid in orientation, wayfinding, group decision-making, knowledge of changing contexts, improved problem-solving (in older children)
findings.quote: Nature provides both the platform and the objects for play (Kahn and Kellert 2002). It encourages exploration and building among older children which aids orientation and wayfinding, group decision-making, knowledge of how to respond to changing contexts, and improved problem-solving.

findings.antecedent: Small-scale natural environments with props (flowers, stones, sticks, water)
findings.consequent: Stimulation of imaginative play (cornerstone of social and cognitive development in younger children)
findings.quote: Among younger children, small-scale natural environments with props (flowers, stones, sticks, water) stimulate imaginative play which is considered a cornerstone of social and cognitive development.

findings.antecedent: Socio-economic status
findings.consequent: Unequal distribution of nature amenities in urban environments (access to parks, street trees, landscaping)
findings.quote: We know from everyday experience that nature is not equitably distributed in urban environments. Those who can afford to do so live near parks, have large street trees and rich landscaping around their homes, and work in places that have design amenities.
